## What it checks

The `stat_p_exact` module flags two kinds of problematic p-values:

- **Imprecise p-values** — for example `p < .05` or `p = n.s.` instead of an exact value like `p = .031`.
- **P-values reported as exactly zero** — for example `p = .000` or `p = 0.00`. A p-value is never exactly zero; `p = .000` is a rounding artifact (the true value is simply smaller than the reported precision) and should be written `p < .001`.

Each detected value carries an `imprecise` flag and a `zero` flag, and either kind turns the traffic light **red**. When a `p = .000` is found, the report includes its own guidance explaining why exactly-zero p-values should be reported as `p < .001`.

Detection is case-insensitive, so an upper-case `P = .04` is found just as reliably as `p = .04`.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged as imprecise:

- a **table note**, such as "\* p < .05, \*\* p < .01", "ns: p > .05" or "† p < .10";
- a **figure legend**, such as "Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)" or "Values in bold are significant at p < .05";
- a **stated threshold**, such as "p < .05 was considered significant", "thresholded at P < .001" or "a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of p < .02".

GROBID often puts table notes and figure legends into the running text, so the section a sentence is in cannot tell them apart from results. Each p-value is therefore judged by the words of its own clause (the text up to a ";" or a full stop), and is never left out when a test statistic belongs to it ("F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05"). The column `not_a_test` of the table says why a p-value was left out (`"marker"`, `"threshold"` or `"legend"`), and is `NA` for the p-values that were judged. Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value ("p < .05 (\*)"), are still flagged.

The words that mark a threshold cannot always tell a sentence that sets a threshold from one that reports a result against it. The module therefore sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set, and it can miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold, such as "decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold". The report says so when it lists imprecise p-values.

Reporting exact p-values is an APA Journal Article Reporting Standard (JARS). It also lets readers include results in p-curve or z-curve meta-analyses and check internal consistency with tools like Statcheck.

This module is **fully offline**.

## Running the module

::: {.callout-note}
## Without R
This module also runs on [Metacheck's website](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/): upload a paper under *Run Metacheck on a Paper*, where it is one of the default checks under *Checks*. The [Docker installation](get-started.qmd#docker-installation) offers the same website on your own computer. The website runs the module with its default settings; to change them, run it in R as below.
:::


```{.r .cell-code}
paper <- demopaper()
module_run(paper, "stat_p_exact")
```

Exact P-Values: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 3 detected *p* values.

The `table` lists every detected p-value, with `imprecise` and `zero` flags, and in `not_a_test` the reason a p-value was left out:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(paper, "stat_p_exact")
mo$traffic_light
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "red"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$summary_text
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 3 detected *p* values."
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$table[, c("text", "p_comp", "p_value", "imprecise", "zero", "not_a_test")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|text      |p_comp | p_value|imprecise |zero  |not_a_test |
|:---------|:------|-------:|:---------|:-----|:----------|
|p = 0.005 |=      |   0.005|FALSE     |FALSE |NA         |
|p =0.152  |=      |   0.152|FALSE     |FALSE |NA         |
|p > .05   |>      |   0.050|TRUE      |FALSE |NA         |


:::
:::


To see only the problematic ones:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$table[mo$table$imprecise | mo$table$zero, c("text", "expanded")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|text    |expanded                                                                                                                                       |
|:-------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|p > .05 |There was no effect of experience on the reduction in errors when using the tool (p > .05), as the correlation was non-significant (Figure 2). |


:::
:::


## Running on many papers

The `summary_table` reports a per-paper count for each problem type: `n_imprecise` (imprecise p-values) and `n_zero` (p-values reported as exactly zero).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(psychsci[1:20], "stat_p_exact")
head(mo$summary_table) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

The p-values in these papers that were left out because they are not the result of a test:

```{.r .cell-code}
not_tests <- mo$table[!is.na(mo$table$not_a_test), c("paper_id", "expanded", "not_a_test")]
head(not_tests, 10) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## A clean example and one with problems

A known paper that reports imprecise p-values:


```{.r .cell-code}
module_run(psychsci$`0956797614560771`, "stat_p_exact")
```

Exact P-Values: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 4 detected *p* values.

A paper that reports a p-value as exactly zero (`p = .000`). This is flagged separately from imprecise values, with its own guidance that exactly-zero p-values should be reported as `p < .001`:


```{.r .cell-code}
module_run(psychsci$`0956797615603702`, "stat_p_exact")
```

Exact P-Values: We found 1 *p* value reported as exactly zero out of 8 detected *p* values.

A paper that reports all p-values exactly returns green:


```{.r .cell-code}
module_run(psychsci$`0956797616665351`, "stat_p_exact")
```

Exact P-Values: We found no imprecise *p* values or *p*-values of exactly zero out of 8 detected.

## Options

`stat_p_exact` takes only the `paper` argument.

## Validation

> In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negatives). 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).
